query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Homogenizing the defect landscape in as‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs reduces the local spread of exchange interaction energies, which in turn broadens the magnetocaloric entropy change peak and minimizes hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA thin films exhibiting a single ordered hexagonal phase with an inherent heterogeneous distribution of lattice defects (e.g., grain boundaries, dislocations) that locally modulate magnetic exchange interactions.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-deposited films to controlled low-energy ion irradiation designed to selectively relax or homogenize point defect and interfacial disorder without altering the overall crystallographic phase.
generation.conditions: Irradiation performed at room temperature with a low fluence (ensuring minimal amorphization) followed by magnetic measurements using low applied fields (<0.2 T) during cooling cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and spatial uniformity of defects (grain-boundary and point defects) that mediate the local variations in exchange interactions.
generation.mechanism: Low-energy ion irradiation homogenizes the defect distribution by healing localized strain concentrations and reducing inhomogeneous defect clusters. This narrows the distribution of magnetic exchange energies, thereby making the magnetostructural transition more gradual and lowering the energy barriers for domain reconfiguration. As a result, the magnetocaloric entropy change becomes less abrupt and less hysteretic under low-field conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated baseline samples, irradiated specimens will show a broadened magnetocaloric peak (i.e., a wider temperature range of significant entropy change) and reduced hysteresis losses during low-applied-field cycling.
generation.baseline: As-deposited films without irradiation that exhibit a sharp, hysteretic magnetocaloric response due to a broad distribution of exchange interactions induced by heterogeneous defect densities.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for as-deposited, rare-earth-free FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA thin films with similar phase purity and defect structure; effects may differ if the material is substantially annealed, mechanically deformed, or processed in bulk forms.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how precisely low-energy ion irradiation will modify the defect landscape in this specific HEA composition without inducing secondary phases. This proposal builds on the observed defect-dependent exchange interaction variations in PMC4623812 (magnetocaloric effect) and PMC8044135 (role of defects in magnetic hysteresis), while extending those findings by applying a controlled irradiation treatment—a method not previously explored in this system. Also, the optimal irradiation dose and potential unintended microstructural changes remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA thin films. Subject one set to low-energy ion irradiation at a calibrated low fluence designed to homogenize defect distribution without altering crystal structure; keep the second set as an untreated control. Characterize both sets using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) line profile analysis to assess defect density and uniformity. Then perform temperature-dependent magnetization measurements and record magnetic entropy change and hysteresis loop characteristics under low-applied fields (<0.2 T) during magnetic cooling cycles.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) versus temperature curves
Hysteresis loop measurements at low applied fields
Defect distribution quantification via TEM/XRD line broadening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the irradiated samples do not show a statistically significant broadening of the ΔS(T) peak and reduction in hysteresis (compared to the control) or if irradiation causes unwanted phase changes, then the hypothesis—that homogenizing the defect landscape reduces the spread of exchange interactions governing magnetocaloric response—is falsified.
